To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

gain-of-function mutations in ryanodine receptors 1 (RYR1) are associated with a variety of neuropsychiatric disorders, including malignant hyperthermias, a pharmacogenetic disease caused by dysregulated release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic retics of skeletal muscle.

a gain-of-function mutation in the RYR gene causes subtle but significant changes in the immune response, suggesting that the immune system is affected by RYR1 mutation, and that these changes might provide selective immune advantages to the mutation carriers.

1) a mutation that causes malignant hyperthermia in mice also causes gain-of-function effects on immune cells, and 2) pharmacological activation of ryanodine receptors might be exploited for development of novel vaccines and adjuvant.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology of a group of neuromuscluar disorders, the so called ‘ryanodine receptor diseases’, and the development of novel therapeutic strategies for their treatment.
the study of the role of ryanodine receptors in the regulation of calcium homeostasis in skeletal muscle and other tissues.
the study of the immune system and its role in the development of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RYR Y522S knock-in mutation causes a gain-of-function in the immune system.
the RYR mutation is a gain of function, and the gain of function is in the immune system.
the RYR-1 mutation Y522S causes a gain-of-function in the immune system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a gain of function mutation in the ryanodine channel of skeletal muscle can also cause a gain of function in the ryanadine channel of immune cells.
the gain-of-function mutation of RYR1 in mice causes an increased Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticular store in skeletal muscle and dendritic cells.
the RYR mutation causes a gain of function of the immune system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mutations in the RYR gene can cause gain of function effects in immune cells, in particular in dendritic cells.
RYR1 can be a target in the development of new vaccines and adjuvant therapies.
a mutation that causes a hypermetabolic disease in one tissue can cause gain of function in a completely unrelated tissue.
